records.sourceFile: Phytochemicals for Improving Aspects of Cognitive Function and Psychological State Potentially Relevant to Sports Performance.pdf

paper.citation: Kennedy DO. Phytochemicals for improving aspects of cognitive function and psychological state potentially relevant to sports performance. Sports Medicine. 2019.
paper.abstract: The review considers phytochemicals from three structural groups (phenolics, terpenes and alkaloids) and their possible effects on alertness, attention, memory and executive function in healthy people. It notes that polyphenols mainly affect cerebral blood flow and cardiovascular health, that several terpene and triterpene extracts show cognitive benefits in single-dose or short trials, and that nicotine and caffeine can enhance cognition at low doses. The author concludes that little of this evidence has been collected in a sporting context.
paper.tldr: This narrative review finds consistent cardiovascular benefits from polyphenols and mixed cognitive results for most compounds. Almost none of the evidence comes from sporting contexts, so it does not support performance claims for athletes.
paper.methods: This is a narrative review with no described search strategy. It summarizes human controlled-trial evidence on cocoa, fruit and single-molecule polyphenols, volatile and non-volatile terpenes, triterpenes, nicotine and caffeine, with dose, duration and outcome reported in the text, and it notes sporting-context evidence separately.
paper.findings: In two matched 4-week trials, a 990 mg flavanol drink improved two attention and executive function tasks in 90 healthy older adults and in 90 adults with age-related cognitive impairment, while several 250 to 750 mg flavanol trials of 4 to 6 weeks in middle-aged and older adults found no cognitive benefit. Single doses of sage extract or essential oil improved memory in healthy adults, peppermint tea improved alertness and memory accuracy in 180 young adults, and a meta-analysis of nine chronic bacopa trials (518 participants, about 300 mg per day) found improved attention and processing speed. For resveratrol, a meta-analysis found benefits in only three of ten studies, and the review identifies a single triterpene study in 15 athletes that improved reaction times.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative selection without a described search, so the choice of studies and the review's judgments of strength (for example 'weak' or 'promising') cannot be checked. Most trials use single doses or short supplementation in healthy non-athletes, and some findings are described as subtle, with the author noting possible publication bias. The review draws no firm conclusions for sport.
paper.practicalImplications: The review supports dietary polyphenols for cardiovascular health, but it does not support using these compounds to improve cognition or performance in sport. It states that no firm recommendations for sport are possible at present, so staff should not present these compounds as performance aids on the basis of this review. The author advises avoiding nicotine because of its addictive properties, and identifies low-dose caffeine combined with other phytochemicals, such as guarana, as an area needing more research.
paper.athleteDev: The review finds very few sport-context trials: one study of 15 athletes found a triterpene extract improved reaction times before and during graded cycling, and one study of 30 participants found peppermint essential oil improved reaction times and some physical performance measures. It reports that caffeine's ergogenic effects in endurance, high-intensity and intermittent exercise are well established, but that little research links caffeine's effect on alertness or attention to sport performance.
paper.rtp: The review does not address injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.
